content: Dr. Samuel William Becker (1894–1964), a dermatologist, is the namesake of Becker's nevus, a skin disorder that predominantly affects males. This condition typically manifests initially as irregular pigmentation, either melanosis or hyperpigmentation, most commonly on the torso or upper arm, although other areas of the body can also be affected. Over time, the lesion enlarges irregularly, becomes thickened, and often develops excessive hair growth, a condition known as hypertrichosis. Becker's nevus is also referred to by several other names, including Becker nevus, Becker's pigmented hairy nevus, Becker pigmented hairy nevus, Becker melanosis, and pigmented hairy epidermal nevus. The medical understanding and documentation of Becker's nevus remain limited. This is likely due to a combination of factors, including its relatively recent identification, low prevalence, and the primarily aesthetic nature of its effects. Consequently, the pathophysiology of Becker's nevus is not well understood. While it is generally considered an acquired condition rather than a congenital one, there has been at least one documented case suggesting a potential genetic association. This case involved a 16-month-old boy with a hyperpigmented lesion on his right shoulder, whose father had a similar lesion in the same location. The most comprehensive study to date, conducted in 1981, surveyed nearly 20,000 young French men and challenged several previously held beliefs about the disorder. It was found that 52% of the lesions appeared before the age of 10, with the remainder developing between the ages of 10 and 20. Sun exposure was implicated in about 25% of cases, a lower percentage than researchers had anticipated. Additionally, contrary to prior assumptions, only 32% of Becker's nevi were located above the nipples, despite the upper chest and shoulder region being thought to be the most common sites. The pigmentation was light brown in 75% of cases, and the average size of the nevus was approximately 125 cm² (19 in²). In terms of malignancy, a 1991 report documented nine cases of patients with both Becker's nevus and malignant melanoma. Of these, five melanomas were located in the same body region as the nevus, but only one occurred within the nevus itself. This was the first documented co-occurrence of the two conditions, and there is currently no evidence to suggest that Becker's nevi have a higher rate of malignancy compared to normal skin. Nevertheless, as with any abnormal skin growth, it is recommended that the nevus be monitored regularly, and any sudden changes in appearance should be promptly evaluated by a healthcare professional. Diagnosis of Becker's nevus is typically made through physical examination, often with reference to dermatological atlases for comparison. Treatment for Becker's nevus is generally not necessary, as it is considered a benign lesion. However, treatment may be sought for cosmetic reasons. Unwanted hair can be managed through shaving or trimming, while laser hair removal may provide a longer-lasting solution. Various laser treatments may also be effective in reducing or eliminating hyperpigmentation, although the outcomes of laser treatments for both hair and pigmentation reduction are highly variable.
